lesson.title: The Fine Print on Hydrogen Bonds
lesson.summary: Hydrogen bonding is not just an attraction to any electronegative atom: it requires a hydrogen covalently bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, and that strict rule explains anomalies like water's unusually high boiling point.
lesson.body:
You already know hydrogen bonding is an unusually strong dipole-dipole attraction. What is easy to miss is how narrow the rule for it actually is. Hydrogen bonding occurs only when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded directly to nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), or fluorine (F) in one molecule, and that hydrogen is then attracted to a lone pair on an N, O, or F atom in a nearby molecule. Chemists often write this as N-H...O or O-H...O or F-H...N, where the solid line is the covalent bond and the dots represent the intermolecular attraction. Notice that both halves matter: a donor hydrogen attached to N, O, or F, and an acceptor atom that is also N, O, or F with a lone pair available.

Why only these three elements? Two properties have to line up at once. First, N, O, and F are among the most electronegative elements on the periodic table, so a bond to hydrogen is sharply polarized, leaving hydrogen with a large partial positive charge. Second, N, O, and F are small atoms. Because the electronegative atom is small, that concentrated positive charge on hydrogen is not shielded by a bulky electron cloud, so it can get close enough to another molecule's lone pair for a genuinely strong attraction to form. Electronegativity without small size gives an ordinary dipole-dipole force, and size without high electronegativity gives almost nothing at all.

This is exactly why chlorine fails the test even though its electronegativity is close to nitrogen's. A useful comparison is water versus hydrogen sulfide. Oxygen and sulfur sit in the same group, so a naive guess might predict similar boiling points, adjusted for sulfur's larger mass. Instead, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius while hydrogen sulfide boils around minus 60 degrees Celsius, a difference of roughly 160 degrees. Sulfur is a much larger, more diffuse atom than oxygen, so an S-H bond cannot generate a true hydrogen bond, only a weaker dipole-dipole attraction. Water's anomalously high boiling point, along with its high melting point and high heat of vaporization, is essentially a hydrogen bonding fingerprint left in its physical properties.

A quick working test: scan a molecule for an H atom bonded directly to N, O, or F. If one exists, that hydrogen can act as a donor. Ammonia (NH3), water (H2O), hydrogen fluoride (HF), methanol (CH3OH), and amines and alcohols in general all qualify. A molecule can also contain N, O, or F without being a donor, if none of its hydrogens sit directly on those atoms; formaldehyde (H2CO) has no O-H bond, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, though its oxygen lone pairs let it accept one from a molecule that can donate, such as water.

Applying the same test to carbon is a common source of errors. Carbon-hydrogen bonds are nearly nonpolar because carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities, so C-H bonds never participate in hydrogen bonding no matter how many N, O, or F atoms sit elsewhere in the molecule. A molecule like acetone, which has plenty of C-H bonds and one C=O, can accept hydrogen bonds through its oxygen lone pairs but cannot donate any, since it has no O-H or N-H bond of its own. Getting this requirement precise matters enormously later, since it is the deciding factor in ranking intermolecular forces and in predicting solubility, boiling point, and even how DNA base pairs recognize each other through matched hydrogen bond donors and acceptors.
